expected_sources.role: Active rural water projects in Eastern and Southern Africa
Tanzania SRWSSP Phase II (PforR + IPF), program appraisal document dated Sep 2025 inside
Kenya Water, Sanitation and Hygiene Program (K-WASH, PforR + IPF)
Ethiopia One WASH Consolidated Account Project; an acceptable further comparator
Zambia Water Supply and Sanitation Services in Growth Centers Program; an acceptable further comparator

text: Active comparable operations (Projects API, Eastern and Southern Africa, rural water): Tanzania Sustainable Rural Water Supply and Sanitation Program Phase II (P508698, approved 2025-09-30, closing 2030-09-30), Kenya Water, Sanitation and Hygiene Program (K-WASH, P179012, approved 2023-12-20, closing 2030-06-30); others include Ethiopia One WASH (P507830), Zambia WSS in Growth Centers (P509550/P179237) and Somalia Barwaaqo rural water resilience (P177627). Two are read below.

Tanzania SRWSSP II - design: hybrid PforR (US$307 million: IDA US$185 million, Government US$100 million, ESMAP US$2 million, US$20 million expected from PPP commercial finance) plus a US$15 million IPF component for technical assistance (p. 57). Three results areas: access and sustainability of basic WASH including schools and health facilities, with climate-resilient design (RA 1, US$141.56 million IDA); policy, institutions and regulation (RA 2); maximizing finance for development (RA 3) (pp. 57-58). It is phase 2 of a regional WASH MPA led at regional level by AUDA-NEPAD (p. 27).

Tanzania SRWSSP II - implementing arrangements: Ministry of Water as program owner, with a National Steering Committee of MoW, MoH, MoEST, PO-RALG, MoF and others; RUWASA oversees rural water investments; MoH leads sanitation and hygiene; districts (supported by regional secretariats) procure and build WASH in schools, health facilities and household sanitation; PO-RALG's 25 regional secretariats backstop 137 district councils; the Internal Auditor General verifies results as Independent Verification Agent; in Zanzibar the Ministry of Water, Energy and Minerals leads (pp. 8, 62).

Kenya K-WASH - design: hybrid operation of US$458 million: PforR US$438 million (IDA US$230 million incl. US$40 million refugee-window grant, Government US$200 million, US$8 million commercial financing by water service providers) plus a US$20 million IPF (pp. 20-21). Covers 19 mainly rural counties selected on marginalization, ASAL status, density, access and open defecation, plus the refugee-hosting Turkana and Garissa (p. 20, fn. 29-30). Results areas start with county policy, institutional and regulatory reforms (a County Water and Sanitation Strategy and Investment Plan) before financing new and rehabilitated schemes with professional O&M models and multiple-use design, and include WSP financial performance reforms (pp. 19-21). It responds to WSP inefficiency (about US$90 million lost a year) and unregulated community schemes with non-cost-reflective tariffs (p. 15).

Kenya K-WASH - implementing arrangements: Ministry of Water, Sanitation and Irrigation (State Department for Water and Sanitation) as implementing agency (p. 7); county governments and county-owned WSPs as the incentivized delivery level; WASREB oversees WSP regulatory compliance (a DLI) and builds county capacity; the Water Sector Trust Fund helps WSPs prepare bankable projects for commercial finance (p. 11).

Common choices relevant to the proposed operation: PforR with an IPF for TA; disbursement tied to subnational performance; sustainability through professionalized O&M and regulation; a role for commercial finance; and independent verification.

right_sources: Identifies active rural water projects in East Africa (from the Projects API) and reads the appraisal documents of at least two (the reference uses P508698 and P179012; other qualifying active projects are acceptable).
grounded: Design choices and arrangements are cited to the appraisal documents with pages; financing figures match.
complete: Covers both design choices and implementing arrangements for each project discussed.
scoped: States which projects were read and why they are comparable.

notes: Cross-project case: other active East African rural water operations are acceptable comparators if grounded.
